lead: This unit explains how Ethereum turns a blockchain into a programmable world computer. You will follow a transaction from wallet to EVM, read and write Solidity contracts, and deploy them on a private net or testnet. By the end you can explain gas, accounts, smart contracts, DApps and the GHOST fork-choice rule in exam-ready terms.
about: Unit 5 covers Ethereum as a programmable blockchain. Chapter 5.1 maps the network and ecosystem. 5.2 separates ether, tokens, signed transactions and internal messages. 5.3 opens the EVM stack machine and gas. 5.4 explains smart contracts and their lifecycle, and 5.5 turns that into Solidity. 5.6 sets up Remix, testnets and a private net. 5.7 connects contracts to Web3, deployment and DApp frameworks. 5.8 is an advanced look at DAOs, the GHOST fork-choice rule and side chains. Each chapter uses one worked numerical example and one figure, so revision moves from a transaction to a deployed DApp.

chapters.idea: Ethereum is a public account-based blockchain run by nodes, and its ecosystem is the set of clients, wallets, tools, tokens and applications built around that network.
chapters.depth: Cover the Ethereum network, nodes and clients, accounts, world state, wallets, block explorers, dApps, testnets and the main ecosystem parts. Distinguish full, archive and light nodes at overview level. Some syllabi call this the components of the Ethereum ecosystem or Ethereum architecture. Keep it conceptual and point forward to ether, EVM and contracts.

figure.title: Ethereum ecosystem path
figure.aria: A user signs a request in a wallet, sends it to an Ethereum node, which gossips it to peer nodes and updates the shared world state.

chapters.example: A wallet shows 2 ETH. The node reports the same 2 ETH balance and nonce 7. The user sends 0.3 ETH to a contract, and the gas fee is 0.001 ETH. Find the user balance, contract balance and user nonce after the transaction. Answer: user balance = 2 − 0.3 − 0.001 = 1.699 ETH; contract balance = 0.3 ETH; nonce = 8.
chapters.trap: Do not treat a wallet as the blockchain. The wallet holds keys and displays a view; the node and world state decide balances and nonces.
chapters.prereq: Unit 1 blockchain networks and nodes; Unit 3 peer-to-peer networks.
chapters.leave: Ether units, transaction fields and messages to 5.2; EVM execution to 5.3; contract code to 5.5.

chapters.idea: Ether is the native currency, tokens are contract records, and a transaction is a signed state change while a message is an internal call inside execution.
chapters.depth: Cover ether units (wei, gwei, ETH), externally owned accounts versus contract accounts, nonce, value, gas limit, gas price and fee fields, transaction lifecycle, receipts, logs, internal messages and token contracts. Explain ETH and ETC as the two chains after the DAO-related fork. Some syllabi call this transactions and messages or ether cryptocurrency and tokens.

figure.aria: A signed transaction moves from user to wallet to node, the EVM executes it, a contract receives an internal message, and a receipt returns to the user.

chapters.example: A transaction uses 21,000 gas at a gas price of 20 gwei and carries a value of 0.1 ETH. Find the fee in ETH and the total ETH debited from the sender. Answer: fee = 21,000 × 20 gwei = 420,000 gwei = 0.00042 ETH; total debit = 0.1 + 0.00042 = 0.10042 ETH.
chapters.trap: Gas price times gas used is the fee, not the value sent. A message is not a signed transaction and does not enter the transaction pool.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 transaction life cycle; Unit 4 digital signatures; 5.1.
chapters.leave: Opcode gas costs to 5.3; Solidity token code to 5.5; deployment to 5.7.

chapters.idea: The EVM is a deterministic, gas-metered stack machine that executes contract bytecode and changes only account state that is committed in a block.
chapters.depth: Cover the EVM as a virtual machine, 256-bit words, stack, memory, storage, calldata, opcodes, gas accounting, call frames, revert and logs. Use PUSH, ADD, MSTORE, SLOAD, SSTORE, CALL and REVERT as named examples without listing every opcode. Some syllabi call this the Ethereum Virtual Machine or EVM execution model. Keep bytecode reading simple.

figure.title: EVM stack for 60 02 60 03 01
figure.aria: Three stack snapshots: 2, then 3 above 2, then the single result 5 after ADD.

chapters.example: Bytecode 60 02 60 03 01 runs as PUSH1 0x02, PUSH1 0x03, ADD. Give the stack after each step and the total gas if PUSH1 costs 3 gas and ADD costs 3 gas. Answer: after PUSH1 2, stack = [2]; after PUSH1 3, stack = [3, 2]; after ADD, stack = [5]; total gas = 3 + 3 + 3 = 9.
chapters.trap: The EVM is a stack machine, not a register machine. Storage is persistent and costly; memory is temporary and expands during a call.
chapters.leave: High-level contract syntax to 5.5; deployment and ABI to 5.7.

chapters.idea: A smart contract is code and state on the blockchain that runs when a transaction calls it and enforces the same rules for every node.
chapters.depth: Cover the smart contract concept, properties, lifecycle, accounts, calls, events, escrow, micropayments and decentralized lottery examples. Explain why contracts are deterministic and why they need oracles for outside data. Some syllabi call this smart contracts and development or contract capabilities. Keep Solidity details for 5.5.

figure.title: Contract lifecycle
figure.aria: A contract moves from written rules to compiled bytecode and ABI, local tests, deployment at an address, and interaction by transactions.

chapters.example: A buyer deposits 1 ETH into an escrow contract. The contract releases the 1 ETH to the seller if the buyer calls confirm within 7 days; otherwise the seller can refund the buyer after 7 days. The buyer confirms on day 3. Ignoring gas, give the contract balance and the seller payment. Answer: contract pays 1 ETH to the seller; contract balance = 0 ETH; seller receives 1 ETH.
chapters.trap: A contract cannot start itself or fetch a web price by itself. It runs only when called, and outside data needs an oracle.
chapters.prereq: 5.3 EVM execution; Unit 4 smart contract examples.
chapters.leave: Solidity syntax to 5.5; testnets to 5.6; deployment frameworks to 5.7.

chapters.idea: Solidity is a statically typed contract language that compiles to EVM bytecode and expresses state, functions, events and access rules.
chapters.depth: Cover pragma, contract, state variables, types such as uint and address, mapping, functions, visibility, modifiers, events, errors and revert, payable, inheritance and storage versus memory. Mention that compiler versions differ, so a pragma is used. Some syllabi call this the Solidity language or smart contract programming. Keep code small and exam-readable.

figure.aria: A SimpleBank contract tree with balances state, deposit and withdraw functions, and a Paid event.

chapters.example: A contract SimpleBank has mapping(address => uint) balances. Alice deposits 0.5 ETH, Bob deposits 0.2 ETH, and Alice withdraws 0.1 ETH. Give Alice balance, Bob balance and total contract balance. Answer: Alice = 0.4 ETH; Bob = 0.2 ETH; contract total = 0.6 ETH.
chapters.trap: A mapping returns zero for an unknown key. Do not confuse address with address payable, or a public variable with a function call.
chapters.prereq: 5.3 EVM storage and gas; 5.4 contract lifecycle.
chapters.leave: Deployment, ABI and Web3 calls to 5.7; DAO governance to 5.8.

chapters.idea: Ethereum development starts on a local chain or testnet, where contracts and private networks can be tested before mainnet.
chapters.depth: Cover Remix IDE, local blockchain tools, faucets, testnets such as Sepolia with a warning that names change, and private net setup: genesis file, chain ID, geth init, start node, create account, send a test transaction and mine. Some syllabi call this Ethereum development environment, test networks and setting up a private net.

figure.title: Private net setup
figure.aria: Private net steps: write a genesis with chainId 1337, initialize geth, start the node, create an account, send 1 ETH, and mine block 1.

chapters.example: A private net genesis sets chainId 1337 and block gas limit 30,000,000. Account A starts with 100 ETH in genesis. A sends 1 ETH to B using 21,000 gas at 1 gwei. Ignoring block rewards, find A and B balances after mining. Answer: fee = 21,000 gwei = 0.000021 ETH; A = 100 − 1 − 0.000021 = 98.999979 ETH; B = 1 ETH.
chapters.trap: Test ether has no market value. A wrong chain ID or genesis file creates a different network, not a connection to mainnet.
chapters.prereq: 5.4 contract lifecycle; 5.5 Solidity; Unit 3 mining and consensus.
chapters.leave: Web3 libraries and DApp deployment to 5.7; production security to 5.8.

chapters.idea: Web3 libraries connect a DApp to an Ethereum node, and frameworks compile, test and deploy contracts through transactions.
chapters.depth: Cover JSON-RPC, providers, signers, Web3.js and ethers.js, ABI, bytecode, contract address, deployment transaction, call versus send, Hardhat and Truffle at overview level, and DApp front-end architecture. Some syllabi call this Web3, contract deployment, development frameworks or DApps using Ethereum. Keep tool commands minimal.

figure.title: DApp call path
figure.aria: A user clicks a DApp UI, the wallet signs a request, an RPC node receives it, and the call reaches the contract at its address.

chapters.example: A contract deployment uses 1,500,000 gas at 20 gwei. Find the deployment fee in ETH. If the deployer starts with 5 ETH and sends 0 value, what remains? Answer: fee = 1,500,000 × 20 gwei = 30,000,000 gwei = 0.03 ETH; remaining balance = 5 − 0.03 = 4.97 ETH.
chapters.trap: A contract needs both its address and ABI to be called correctly. A read call is not a transaction; a state-changing send is.
chapters.prereq: 5.2 transactions and messages; 5.5 Solidity; 5.6 test environment.
chapters.leave: DAO and side-chain design to 5.8; enterprise frameworks to Unit 6.

chapters.idea: A DAO is an organization run by contract rules and voting, GHOST chooses the heaviest block subtree instead of only the longest chain, and side chains extend capacity with separate security.
chapters.depth: Only a few universities teach this chapter. Cover DAO definition, proposals, voting and the reentrancy risk shown by The DAO attack; GHOST weights and uncle blocks; side chains, bridges and their security limits. Mention vulnerability attacks briefly. Keep it shorter than the core chapters and avoid full code.

figure.aria: GHOST block tree: B has subtree weight 4 against uncle U1 weight 1; C has weight 2 against uncle U2 weight 1.

chapters.example: A block tree has root A. A has children B and U1. B has children C and U2. C has child D. Under GHOST, each block weight is the count of blocks in its subtree including itself. Which child of A is chosen, and which child of B? Answer: B subtree = B, C, U2, D = 4; U1 = 1, so choose B. C subtree = C, D = 2; U2 = 1, so choose C.
chapters.trap: GHOST is not the longest-chain rule. A side chain does not automatically inherit mainnet security; its bridge and validators add risk.
chapters.prereq: Unit 3 forks and consensus; 5.1 Ethereum network.
chapters.leave: Namecoin details to Unit 4; scalability and enterprise platforms to Unit 6.
